# Prediction, Compression, and Discovery Are Different Goals

The lasso fits a regression model while shrinking some coefficients exactly to
zero. The resulting rule can be easier to store and inspect than an unpenalized
high-dimensional model. The elastic net combines lasso and ridge penalties,
often improving prediction when useful predictors occur in correlated groups.

Exact zeros are an optimization property, not proof that the discarded
variables are biologically irrelevant or that the retained variables are causal.
Several correlated genes may carry nearly interchangeable information, so small
changes in donors or preprocessing can change which one is selected while
predictions remain similar. Prediction, sparse representation, and biological
discovery therefore require different validation arguments.

# Data-generating Model and Regularized Estimator

For independent experimental units, begin with the linear conditional-mean model

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\mathbf x_i^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol\beta+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad E(\varepsilon_i\mid\mathbf x_i)=0.
$$

After centering the outcome and design, the lasso estimator is

$$
\boxed{
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{lasso}}
=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}
\left\{\frac{1}{2n}\|\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\|_2^2
+\lambda\|\boldsymbol\beta\|_1\right\},
}
$$

where $\|\boldsymbol\beta\|_1=\sum_j|\beta_j|$ and $\lambda\geq0$. The
intercept is normally unpenalized. Package conventions differ in the scaling of
the loss and penalty, so the numerical value of $\lambda$ is software specific.

The elastic net solves

$$
\boxed{
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\lambda,\alpha}
=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}
\left\{\frac{1}{2n}\|\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\|_2^2
+\lambda\left[
\alpha\|\boldsymbol\beta\|_1
+\frac{1-\alpha}{2}\|\boldsymbol\beta\|_2^2
\right]\right\}.
}
$$

Here $\alpha=1$ gives the lasso and $\alpha=0$ gives ridge under this
parameterization; values between zero and one mix sparsity with quadratic
stabilization. Both estimators are biased and depend on the training sample,
preprocessing, candidate feature set, and tuning procedure.

# Why the Lasso Produces Exact Zeros

The absolute-value penalty has a corner at zero. For a standardized orthogonal
design satisfying $\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf X/n=\mathbf I$, let
$z_j=\mathbf x_j^\mathsf{T}\mathbf y/n$ be the unpenalized coefficient. The
lasso solution separates by coordinate:

$$
\widehat\beta_j
=S(z_j,\lambda)
=\operatorname{sign}(z_j)(|z_j|-\lambda)_+.
$$

This **soft-thresholding** rule sets $\widehat\beta_j=0$ when
$|z_j|\leq\lambda$ and otherwise shrinks its magnitude by $\lambda$.

For a general design, the Karush--Kuhn--Tucker conditions are

$$
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf x_j^\mathsf{T}
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
=\lambda s_j,
$$

where $s_j=\operatorname{sign}(\widehat\beta_j)$ for a nonzero coefficient and
$s_j\in[-1,1]$ at zero. Thus an excluded variable has residual correlation no
larger than the penalty threshold. This condition is conditional on all other
selected variables and does not mean that the variable has no population
association.

The constrained form limits $\|\boldsymbol\beta\|_1$. Its diamond-shaped
boundary has corners on coordinate axes, making exact zeros common where loss
contours touch the constraint. Adding the elastic-net $L_2$ term rounds and
stabilizes the problem while retaining corners from the $L_1$ component.

# Correlated Predictors and the Elastic Net

When several predictors are strongly correlated, the lasso may select one and
discard the others, with the identity of the selected feature changing across
resamples. If $p>n$ and the design is in general position, a lasso solution has
at most $n$ nonzero coefficients; ties and rank deficiencies can also make the
coefficient solution nonunique even when fitted values are unique.

The quadratic component of the elastic net encourages correlated predictors to
have more similar coefficients and makes the objective strictly convex in more
settings. This **grouping effect** is useful when a biological signal is spread
over correlated genes, but it does not discover known pathways automatically.
Structured penalties such as group lasso, sparse-group lasso, or graph-guided
penalties are needed when groups or networks should enter the model explicitly.

Elastic net still requires a choice of representation. One-hot indicators,
spline bases, gene summaries, interactions, and compositional coordinates are
different design columns. Penalizing individual columns can violate hierarchy or
select arbitrary levels of a categorical factor. Encode scientifically coherent
term blocks before fitting.

# Tuning $\lambda$ and $\alpha$

Cross-validation commonly selects the penalty parameters for prediction. A
valid procedure must include the whole learning pipeline inside each training
fold:

1. define folds by independent experimental unit;
2. learn imputation, normalization, transformations, feature filters, and scales
   from the training portion only;
3. fit every candidate $(\alpha,\lambda)$ on that processed training portion;
4. evaluate the prespecified loss on the held-out units;
5. use an outer resampling layer or locked test set for performance assessment
   after tuning.

For a binary or count outcome, deviance may align better with the likelihood
than misclassification error or raw squared error. Area under the ROC curve does
not assess probability calibration. Choose the loss from the intended use,
including the relative costs of errors when relevant.

The penalty path should include a sufficiently large $\lambda$ that makes all
penalized coefficients zero and a sufficiently small value approaching the
unpenalized or weakly penalized fit. Tune $\alpha$ as well as $\lambda$ when the
ridge--lasso balance is not fixed prospectively. Because fold assignments add
Monte Carlo variation, inspect repeated grouped cross-validation and the entire
error surface rather than treating one minimizing pair as exact.

# Coefficients, Selection, and Uncertainty

Lasso and elastic-net coefficients are conditional on the penalty and have no
ordinary least-squares sampling distribution. Naive standard errors computed as
if the selected variables had been fixed in advance omit selection uncertainty
and are generally too optimistic. The same data were used both to choose a
model and to estimate its coefficients.

Possible goals require different approaches:

| Goal | Appropriate evidence | Important limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Predict new units | nested validation or a locked external test set | performance can shift across sites or populations |
| Obtain a compact rule | report the complete preprocessing and fitted coefficients | sparsity can be unstable |
| Describe feature stability | repeated subsampling or stability selection | frequencies depend on algorithm and tuning choices |
| Estimate a prespecified effect | design-based model with justified adjustment and uncertainty | prediction penalties need not target causal effects |
| Test post-selection hypotheses | valid selective, debiased, sample-splitting, or external-confirmation method | each method adds assumptions and may lose power |

Refitting an unpenalized model on lasso-selected features can reduce shrinkage
bias, but it does not erase selection bias. If selection and refitting use the
same outcomes, ordinary p-values remain invalid. Sample splitting separates the
two tasks at the cost of information; external confirmation is often more
convincing for biomarker discovery.

# Standardization and Penalty Design

Because both penalties depend on coefficient magnitude, predictors measured on
larger numerical scales are penalized differently unless the design is scaled.
Unit-standard-deviation scaling is common but not automatically scientifically
neutral. Binary indicators, rare variants, pathway scores, and continuous
measurements can warrant different treatment.

Estimate all scaling parameters within training folds and save them with the
deployed model. Do not penalize the intercept. Required design covariates or
known confounders can be assigned zero penalty, but doing so changes the fitted
model and should be declared in advance. Penalty weights can incorporate prior
information, yet outcome-guided tweaking of those weights adds another selection
layer that validation must reproduce.

The lasso also has a Bayesian mode interpretation under independent Laplace
priors; the elastic net corresponds to a combined Laplace--Gaussian penalty.
This analogy does not supply posterior uncertainty when tuning parameters are
selected by cross-validation. A complete Bayesian model treats prior scales and
posterior prediction explicitly.

# Diagnostics and Sensitivity Analysis

Regularization changes coefficient estimation, not the need to diagnose the
data-generating model.

| Threat | Diagnostic or sensitivity check | Consequence if ignored |
|---|---|---|
| Dependence or pseudoreplication | group folds by donor, organism, site, family, or batch as appropriate | validation error is optimistic |
| Leakage | repeat every supervised and unsupervised learned transformation within folds | held-out outcomes indirectly influence training |
| Nonlinearity or wrong likelihood | residual checks, calibration, flexible prespecified terms | penalty cannot repair a wrong mean or variance model |
| Selection instability | selection frequencies and coefficient paths over repeated resamples | a printed sparse list overstates certainty |
| Dataset shift | external validation and covariate-support comparisons | in-domain accuracy need not transport |
| Class imbalance | inspect calibration and decision-relevant metrics | accuracy can hide poor minority-class performance |
| Penalty dependence | vary $\alpha$, scaling, feature filters, and fold definitions | conclusions may be artifacts of one pipeline choice |

Also inspect missingness, influential units, prediction residuals, calibration by
relevant subgroups, and whether external observations lie inside the training
predictor support. A sparse coefficient path is not a goodness-of-fit diagnostic.

# Worked Bioinformatics Example

Consider predicting treatment response from 20,000 transcript measurements in
150 patients, with two sequencing libraries per patient. Patients, not libraries
or reads, are the independent experimental units. Library replicates can improve
measurement precision, but placing replicates from one patient in different
folds leaks patient-specific signal.

A defensible elastic-net pipeline keeps each patient's libraries together,
performs normalization and any variance filter inside the training folds, tunes
$\alpha$ and $\lambda$ in an inner grouped loop, and evaluates the frozen
pipeline in outer held-out patients. Batch, treatment center, and prespecified
clinical predictors are handled according to the intended deployment setting;
they are not dropped merely because a penalized coefficient is zero.

Statistically, stable external prediction supports the complete algorithm for a
defined target population. A gene selected in 70% of resamples has algorithmic
selection stability under that resampling scheme; it does not have a 70%
probability of being causal. Biologically, claims about mechanism need independent
replication, perturbation, and attention to correlated pathways and tissue
composition.

# Connections and Take-home Messages

- [Ridge regression](ridge-regression.qmd) provides the quadratic component and
  singular-value view of shrinkage.
- [Multicollinearity and identifiability](../regression-models/multicollinearity-and-identifiability.qmd)
  explains why correlated designs destabilize individual coefficients.
- [Variable selection and nested-model testing](../regression-models/variable-selection-and-nested-model-testing.qmd)
  separates adaptive search from prespecified tests.
- [Cross-validation](../regression-models/cross-validation.qmd) and
  [train, validation, and test-set design](../regression-models/train-validation-and-test-set-design.qmd)
  cover honest tuning and performance evaluation.
- [Separation and instability in logistic regression](../regression-models/separation-and-instability-in-logistic-regression.qmd)
  describes a setting in which penalties can produce finite predictive fits.
- [Sensitivity analysis and robustness](../statistical-inference/sensitivity-analysis-and-robustness.qmd)
  provides a framework for pipeline perturbations.

1. The lasso uses an $L_1$ penalty to shrink and select; the elastic net adds an
   $L_2$ component that stabilizes correlated-feature fits.
2. Exact zero coefficients describe a fitted optimization solution, not absence
   of biological relevance or causality.
3. Preprocessing, feature filtering, scaling, and tuning must occur within folds
   defined at the independent-unit level.
4. Sparse models can predict well while selecting unstable feature sets; report
   both predictive uncertainty and selection stability.
5. Post-selection inference requires methods that account for the adaptive
   search or independent confirmation data.
